Measurable fields of Hilbert spaces and their direct integrals

Written by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), September 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI. Original text: CC0 1.0.

A direct integral of Hilbert spaces is a continuous version of a direct sum. One attaches a Hilbert space H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) to each point γ\gammaγ of a measure space and forms the space of square-integrable sections γ↦ξ(γ)∈H(γ)\gamma\mapsto\xi(\gamma)\in H(\gamma)γ↦ξ(γ)∈H(γ). When all fibres equal one separable space K\mathcal KK, this is L2(Γ,μ;K)L^2(\Gamma,\mu;\mathcal K)L2(Γ,μ;K). When the base is countable, it is a weighted direct sum. Direct integrals are the standard tool for decomposing representations and von Neumann algebras into simpler pieces. The spectral theorem, for instance, can be stated this way: a self-adjoint operator on a separable Hilbert space is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by the variable on a direct integral of Hilbert spaces over its spectrum.

The difficulty is measurability. The fibres are different spaces, their dimension may vary from point to point, and some of them may be zero. So there is no single space in which to measure a section. The remedy is to fix a space of sections that count as measurable, subject to three axioms. This lesson develops that framework over an arbitrary σ\sigmaσ-finite measure space. Sections 2 to 5 treat fields of Hilbert spaces: the axioms, measurable orthonormal bases and the dimension function, a criterion that generates a field from a sequence of sections, fields of subspaces, and the identification of a field with a constant field on each set where the dimension is constant. Sections 6 and 7 treat measurable fields of bounded operators, conjugate fields and direct sums. Sections 8 to 10 construct the direct integral Hilbert space and study the diagonal and the decomposable operators on it. Section 11 works out four examples, among them the field of GNS spaces over the quasi-state space of a separable C*-algebra, and Section 12 has exercises with solutions.

We assume measure and integration theory and the elementary theory of Hilbert spaces. Example 11.2 uses the Hilbert tensor product from Spatial tensor products of von Neumann algebras, and Example 11.4 uses the GNS construction. The facts we use without proof are stated in full near the end, in the section Background used without proof.

Direct integrals go back to von Neumann's reduction theory (1949; see [Blackadar, Section III.1.6]), and the axioms for measurable fields used here are Dixmier's. Other basic references are [Takesaki I] and [Blackadar].

1. Conventions

Throughout, (Γ,Σ,μ)(\Gamma,\Sigma,\mu)(Γ,Σ,μ) is a σ\sigmaσ-finite measure space, and measurable means Σ\SigmaΣ-measurable. We do not assume that μ\muμ is complete or that Γ\GammaΓ is a standard Borel space, and we make no countability assumption on Σ\SigmaΣ, except in Theorem 9.1(3), which says so. When Σ\SigmaΣ is complete for μ\muμ, "measurable" means "μ\muμ-measurable" in the usual sense.

Hilbert spaces are complex, inner products are linear in the first variable, and the zero space is allowed. The Gaussian rationals Q+iQ\mathbb Q+i\mathbb QQ+iQ form a countable dense subset of C\mathbb CC.

Let (H(γ))γ∈Γ(H(\gamma))_{\gamma\in\Gamma}(H(γ))γ∈Γ​ be a family of Hilbert spaces. A section is a map ξ\xiξ with ξ(γ)∈H(γ)\xi(\gamma)\in H(\gamma)ξ(γ)∈H(γ) for every γ\gammaγ. Under pointwise operations the sections form a vector space, ∏γH(γ)\prod_\gamma H(\gamma)∏γ​H(γ). For sections ξ,η\xi,\etaξ,η we write ⟨ξ,η⟩\langle\xi,\eta\rangle⟨ξ,η⟩ for the function γ↦⟨ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩\gamma\mapsto\langle\xi(\gamma),\eta(\gamma)\rangleγ↦⟨ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩, and ∥ξ∥\|\xi\|∥ξ∥ for the function γ↦∥ξ(γ)∥\gamma\mapsto\|\xi(\gamma)\|γ↦∥ξ(γ)∥.

2. Measurable fields of Hilbert spaces

Definition 2.1 (Measurable field of Hilbert spaces). A measurable field of Hilbert spaces over (Γ,Σ,μ)(\Gamma,\Sigma,\mu)(Γ,Σ,μ) is a family (H(γ))γ∈Γ(H(\gamma))_{\gamma\in\Gamma}(H(γ))γ∈Γ​ together with a linear subspace M⊆∏γH(γ)\mathfrak M\subseteq\prod_\gamma H(\gamma)M⊆∏γ​H(γ), whose elements are called measurable sections, such that:

  • (F1) for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M, the function ∥ξ∥\|\xi\|∥ξ∥ is measurable;
  • (F2) (saturation) a section η\etaη belongs to M\mathfrak MM whenever ⟨η,ξ⟩\langle\eta,\xi\rangle⟨η,ξ⟩ is measurable for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M;
  • (F3) there is a sequence (ξn)n≥1(\xi_n)_{n\geq1}(ξn​)n≥1​ in M\mathfrak MM such that, for every γ\gammaγ, the vectors ξn(γ)\xi_n(\gamma)ξn​(γ) have dense linear span in H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ). Such a sequence is called fundamental.

Reference: [Takesaki I, Definition IV.8.9] works with μ\muμ-measurable sections over a Borel space with a σ\sigmaσ-finite measure, that is, with the completion of the Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra; Definition 2.1 allows any σ\sigmaσ-algebra.

By (F3) every fibre H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) is separable: the finite combinations of the ξn(γ)\xi_n(\gamma)ξn​(γ) with Gaussian-rational coefficients are dense. Exercise 12.1 shows that (F2) does not follow from (F1) and (F3).

Lemma 2.2 (Closure properties). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M be a measurable field.

  1. For ξ,η∈M\xi,\eta\in\mathfrak Mξ,η∈M, the function ⟨ξ,η⟩\langle\xi,\eta\rangle⟨ξ,η⟩ is measurable.
  2. If f:Γ→Cf:\Gamma\to\mathbb Cf:Γ→C is measurable and ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M, then fξ∈Mf\xi\in\mathfrak Mfξ∈M.
  3. If ξk∈M\xi_k\in\mathfrak Mξk​∈M and ξk(γ)→ξ(γ)\xi_k(\gamma)\to\xi(\gamma)ξk​(γ)→ξ(γ) weakly in H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) for every γ\gammaγ, then ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M.
  4. (Gluing) If (Γk)(\Gamma_k)(Γk​) is a countable measurable partition of Γ\GammaΓ and ξ(k)∈M\xi^{(k)}\in\mathfrak Mξ(k)∈M, the section equal to ξ(k)\xi^{(k)}ξ(k) on Γk\Gamma_kΓk​ belongs to M\mathfrak MM.

Proof. (1) Since M\mathfrak MM is a linear subspace, ξ+ikη∈M\xi+i^k\eta\in\mathfrak Mξ+ikη∈M for k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3. The polarization identity ⟨ξ,η⟩=14∑k=03ik∥ξ+ikη∥2\langle\xi,\eta\rangle=\tfrac14\sum_{k=0}^3 i^k\|\xi+i^k\eta\|^2⟨ξ,η⟩=41​∑k=03​ik∥ξ+ikη∥2 expresses ⟨ξ,η⟩\langle\xi,\eta\rangle⟨ξ,η⟩ through four functions that are measurable by (F1).

(2) For every η∈M\eta\in\mathfrak Mη∈M, the function ⟨fξ,η⟩=f⟨ξ,η⟩\langle f\xi,\eta\rangle=f\langle\xi,\eta\rangle⟨fξ,η⟩=f⟨ξ,η⟩ is measurable by (1). Saturation (F2) gives fξ∈Mf\xi\in\mathfrak Mfξ∈M.

4. Fields of subspaces and measurable projections

Proposition 4.1 (Subspace fields). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M be a measurable field with fundamental sequence (ξn)(\xi_n)(ξn​). Let (ηj)(\eta_j)(ηj​) be a sequence in M\mathfrak MM, and let K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ) be the closed linear span of {ηj(γ)}\{\eta_j(\gamma)\}{ηj​(γ)}.

  1. Let P(γ)P(\gamma)P(γ) be the orthogonal projection of H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) onto K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ). Then Pξ∈MP\xi\in\mathfrak MPξ∈M for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M.
  2. (K(γ))(K(\gamma))(K(γ)) with MK={ξ∈M: ξ(γ)∈K(γ) for all γ}\mathfrak M_K=\{\xi\in\mathfrak M:\ \xi(\gamma)\in K(\gamma)\ \text{for all }\gamma\}MK​={ξ∈M: ξ(γ)∈K(γ) for all γ} is a measurable field with fundamental sequence (ηj)(\eta_j)(ηj​). In particular γ↦dim⁡K(γ)\gamma\mapsto\dim K(\gamma)γ↦dimK(γ) is measurable.
  3. The orthogonal complements K(γ)⊥K(\gamma)^\perpK(γ)⊥, with {ξ∈M: ξ(γ)⊥K(γ) for all γ}\{\xi\in\mathfrak M:\ \xi(\gamma)\perp K(\gamma)\ \text{for all }\gamma\}{ξ∈M: ξ(γ)⊥K(γ) for all γ}, form a measurable field with fundamental sequence ((1−P)ξn)((1-P)\xi_n)((1−P)ξn​).

Proof. Run the recursion from the proof of Theorem 3.1 on the sequence (ηj)(\eta_j)(ηj​) inside M\mathfrak MM. Totality was used there only at the end, to identify the closed span of the new vectors with the whole fibre. So the recursion produces sections fk∈Mf_k\in\mathfrak Mfk​∈M whose nonzero values are orthonormal and have a closed span containing every ηj(γ)\eta_j(\gamma)ηj​(γ). Each fk(γ)f_k(\gamma)fk​(γ) lies in K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ), because the recursion gives fkf_kfk​ the form of Theorem 3.1(2): at each point it is a finite combination of the ηj(γ)\eta_j(\gamma)ηj​(γ). So the nonzero values of the fkf_kfk​ form an orthonormal basis of K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ) at each point. Then Pξ=∑k⟨ξ,fk⟩fkP\xi=\sum_k\langle\xi,f_k\rangle f_kPξ=∑k​⟨ξ,fk​⟩fk​ is a pointwise norm-convergent series. Its terms lie in M\mathfrak MM by Lemma 2.2(1)–(2), so Pξ∈MP\xi\in\mathfrak MPξ∈M by Lemma 2.2(3). This proves (1).

For (2), MK\mathfrak M_KMK​ is a linear subspace satisfying (F1). For (F2), let ζ\zetaζ be a section of (K(γ))(K(\gamma))(K(γ)) such that ⟨ζ,ξ⟩\langle\zeta,\xi\rangle⟨ζ,ξ⟩ is measurable for every ξ∈MK\xi\in\mathfrak M_Kξ∈MK​. For arbitrary ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M we have ⟨ζ,ξ⟩=⟨ζ,Pξ⟩\langle\zeta,\xi\rangle=\langle\zeta,P\xi\rangle⟨ζ,ξ⟩=⟨ζ,Pξ⟩, because ζ(γ)∈K(γ)\zeta(\gamma)\in K(\gamma)ζ(γ)∈K(γ), and Pξ∈MKP\xi\in\mathfrak M_KPξ∈MK​ by (1). So ⟨ζ,ξ⟩\langle\zeta,\xi\rangle⟨ζ,ξ⟩ is measurable for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M. Then (F2) for the ambient field gives ζ∈M\zeta\in\mathfrak Mζ∈M, hence ζ∈MK\zeta\in\mathfrak M_Kζ∈MK​. The ηj\eta_jηj​ form a fundamental sequence by definition of K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ). The dimension function is measurable by Theorem 3.1(1), applied to this field.

Part (3) is the same argument with 1−P1-P1−P in place of PPP. The vectors (1−P(γ))ξn(γ)(1-P(\gamma))\xi_n(\gamma)(1−P(γ))ξn​(γ) are total in K(γ)⊥K(\gamma)^\perpK(γ)⊥, because the ξn(γ)\xi_n(\gamma)ξn​(γ) are total in H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) and 1−P(γ)1-P(\gamma)1−P(γ) maps H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) continuously onto K(γ)⊥K(\gamma)^\perpK(γ)⊥. □\square□

Remark 4.2 (Null sets). Suppose we only know that the vectors ηj(γ)\eta_j(\gamma)ηj​(γ) span a dense subspace of some intended subspace K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ) for γ\gammaγ outside a measurable null set NNN. Apply Proposition 4.1 to the sections 1Γ∖Nηj1_{\Gamma\setminus N}\eta_j1Γ∖N​ηj​. The resulting projection field is measurable, and it agrees with the projection onto K(γ)K(\gamma)K(γ) almost everywhere. For operators on the direct integral this is enough, because measurable fields that agree almost everywhere define the same operator (Theorem 10.1(2)). This situation arises, for instance, when certain sections are known to be dense in the graphs of a field of closed operators only at almost every point.

5. Reduction to constant fields

For d∈{0,1,2,…,∞}d\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,\infty\}d∈{0,1,2,…,∞}, let ℓd2\ell^2_dℓd2​ be Cd\mathbb C^dCd (ℓ2(N)\ell^2(\mathbb N)ℓ2(N) when d=∞d=\inftyd=∞) with standard orthonormal basis (εk)(\varepsilon_k)(εk​).

Theorem 5.1 (Reduction to constant fields). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M be a measurable field, let n(γ)=dim⁡H(γ)n(\gamma)=\dim H(\gamma)n(γ)=dimH(γ), and let Γd={γ:n(γ)=d}\Gamma_d=\{\gamma: n(\gamma)=d\}Γd​={γ:n(γ)=d}. These sets form a countable measurable partition of Γ\GammaΓ. Let (ek)(e_k)(ek​) be an orthonormal fundamental sequence as in Theorem 3.1(1), and define for γ∈Γd\gamma\in\Gamma_dγ∈Γd​ U(γ):H(γ)→ℓd2,U(γ)v=∑k≤d⟨v,ek(γ)⟩εk.(5.1) U(\gamma):H(\gamma)\to\ell^2_d,\qquad U(\gamma)v=\sum_{k\leq d}\langle v,e_k(\gamma)\rangle\varepsilon_k . \tag{5.1} U(γ):H(γ)→ℓd2​,U(γ)v=k≤d∑​⟨v,ek​(γ)⟩εk​.(5.1) Each U(γ)U(\gamma)U(γ) is unitary. A section ξ\xiξ is measurable if and only if, for every ddd, all coordinates γ↦⟨U(γ)ξ(γ),εk⟩\gamma\mapsto\langle U(\gamma)\xi(\gamma),\varepsilon_k\rangleγ↦⟨U(γ)ξ(γ),εk​⟩ are measurable on Γd\Gamma_dΓd​. Consequently, the restriction of the field to Γd\Gamma_dΓd​ is carried by the measurable unitary field UUU onto the constant field ℓd2\ell^2_dℓd2​, whose measurable sections are the maps Γd→ℓd2\Gamma_d\to\ell^2_dΓd​→ℓd2​ with measurable coordinates.

Proof. The partition is measurable because the dimension function is measurable (Theorem 3.1(1)). U(γ)U(\gamma)U(γ) maps an orthonormal basis onto an orthonormal basis, so it is unitary. On Γd\Gamma_dΓd​, the coordinates of UξU\xiUξ are the functions ⟨ξ,ek⟩\langle\xi,e_k\rangle⟨ξ,ek​⟩, k≤dk\leq dk≤d. If ξ\xiξ is measurable, they are measurable by Lemma 2.2(1). Conversely, suppose they are measurable on every Γd\Gamma_dΓd​, and fix kkk. On Γd\Gamma_dΓd​ with d≥kd\geq kd≥k, the function ⟨ξ,ek⟩\langle\xi,e_k\rangle⟨ξ,ek​⟩ is one of these coordinates. On Γd\Gamma_dΓd​ with d<kd<kd<k it vanishes, because ek(γ)=0e_k(\gamma)=0ek​(γ)=0 there. So ⟨ξ,ek⟩=∑d1Γd⟨ξ,ek⟩\langle\xi,e_k\rangle=\sum_d1_{\Gamma_d}\langle\xi,e_k\rangle⟨ξ,ek​⟩=∑d​1Γd​​⟨ξ,ek​⟩ is measurable on Γ\GammaΓ. The Parseval argument in the proof of Theorem 3.1(3) then shows that ⟨ξ,ζ⟩\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle⟨ξ,ζ⟩ is measurable for every ζ∈M\zeta\in\mathfrak Mζ∈M, and (F2) gives ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M. For the constant field, the constant sections εk\varepsilon_kεk​ form a fundamental sequence with constant Gram functions, and Theorem 3.1(4) identifies its measurable sections with the maps that have measurable coordinates. □\square□

Remark 5.2. A map into the separable space ℓd2\ell^2_dℓd2​ with measurable coordinates is weakly measurable, by Parseval's identity. By Pettis's theorem (see Background used without proof), it is then Borel measurable and a pointwise limit of measurable maps with finitely many values. So in the constant case the usual notions of measurability agree. One can also embed all fibres at once into one fixed infinite-dimensional Hilbert space by a measurable field of isometries. That form uses a Borel structure on the set of closed subspaces, and it is treated in The Effros Borel structure. The form above, on the sets of constant dimension, needs no Borel structure on spaces of subspaces, and it is the form used in later lessons.

6. Measurable fields of bounded operators

Definition 6.1 (Measurable operator field). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M and (K(γ)),N(K(\gamma)),\mathfrak N(K(γ)),N be measurable fields. A family x=(x(γ))x=(x(\gamma))x=(x(γ)) with x(γ)∈B(H(γ),K(γ))x(\gamma)\in B(H(\gamma),K(\gamma))x(γ)∈B(H(γ),K(γ)) is a measurable field of bounded operators if the section xξ:γ↦x(γ)ξ(γ)x\xi:\gamma\mapsto x(\gamma)\xi(\gamma)xξ:γ↦x(γ)ξ(γ) belongs to N\mathfrak NN for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M. No bound on ∥x(γ)∥\|x(\gamma)\|∥x(γ)∥ that is uniform in γ\gammaγ is assumed.

Theorem 6.2 (Properties of measurable operator fields). Let xxx be a family of bounded operators as in Definition 6.1.

  1. (Testing) xxx is measurable if and only if xξj∈Nx\xi_j\in\mathfrak Nxξj​∈N for every member of one fundamental sequence (ξj)(\xi_j)(ξj​) of M\mathfrak MM.
  2. (Adjoints) If xxx is measurable, so is x∗=(x(γ)∗)x^*=(x(\gamma)^*)x∗=(x(γ)∗) from (K(γ))(K(\gamma))(K(γ)) to (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)).
  3. (Norms) If xxx is measurable, the function γ↦∥x(γ)∥∈[0,∞)\gamma\mapsto\|x(\gamma)\|\in[0,\infty)γ↦∥x(γ)∥∈[0,∞) is measurable.
  4. (Algebra) Sums, products with measurable scalar functions, and composites of measurable operator fields are measurable. The identity field and the projection fields of Proposition 4.1 are measurable.

Proof. (1) Necessity is clear. For sufficiency, apply Theorem 3.1(2) to the fundamental sequence (ξj)(\xi_j)(ξj​). It gives ek=∑jckjξje_k=\sum_jc_{kj}\xi_jek​=∑j​ckj​ξj​ with measurable coefficients, only finitely many of them nonzero at each point. Hence xek=∑jckj xξjxe_k=\sum_jc_{kj}\,x\xi_jxek​=∑j​ckj​xξj​ is a countable sum of sections of N\mathfrak NN, with finitely many nonzero terms at each point, and it lies in N\mathfrak NN by Lemma 2.2(2)–(3). Now let ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M. The expansion ξ(γ)=∑k⟨ξ,ek⟩(γ)ek(γ)\xi(\gamma)=\sum_k\langle\xi,e_k\rangle(\gamma)e_k(\gamma)ξ(γ)=∑k​⟨ξ,ek​⟩(γ)ek​(γ) converges in norm, and x(γ)x(\gamma)x(γ) is bounded, so xξ=∑k⟨ξ,ek⟩ xek x\xi=\sum_k\langle\xi,e_k\rangle\,xe_k xξ=k∑​⟨ξ,ek​⟩xek​ converges pointwise in norm. Each term lies in N\mathfrak NN by Lemma 2.2(1)–(2), so xξ∈Nx\xi\in\mathfrak Nxξ∈N by Lemma 2.2(3).

(2) For η∈N\eta\in\mathfrak Nη∈N and ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M, ⟨x∗η,ξ⟩=⟨η,xξ⟩\langle x^*\eta,\xi\rangle=\langle\eta,x\xi\rangle⟨x∗η,ξ⟩=⟨η,xξ⟩, which is measurable by Lemma 2.2(1) because xξ∈Nx\xi\in\mathfrak Nxξ∈N. Saturation (F2) for M\mathfrak MM gives x∗η∈Mx^*\eta\in\mathfrak Mx∗η∈M.

(3) Let (ek)(e_k)(ek​) be an orthonormal fundamental sequence of M\mathfrak MM (Theorem 3.1(1)). Let QQQ be the countable set of finitely supported sequences q=(q1,…,qm)q=(q_1,\ldots,q_m)q=(q1​,…,qm​) of Gaussian rationals with ∑∣qk∣2≤1\sum|q_k|^2\leq1∑∣qk​∣2≤1, and let vq=∑kqkek∈Mv_q=\sum_kq_ke_k\in\mathfrak Mvq​=∑k​qk​ek​∈M. Moreover {vq(γ):q∈Q}\{v_q(\gamma):q\in Q\}{vq​(γ):q∈Q} is dense in the closed unit ball of H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ). Since x(γ)x(\gamma)x(γ) is continuous, ∥x(γ)∥=sup⁡q∈Q∥x(γ)vq(γ)∥,(6.1) \|x(\gamma)\|=\sup_{q\in Q}\|x(\gamma)v_q(\gamma)\|, \tag{6.1} ∥x(γ)∥=q∈Qsup​∥x(γ)vq​(γ)∥,(6.1) a countable supremum of functions that are measurable by (F1) for N\mathfrak NN. 7. Conjugate fields, direct sums and block operators

Proposition 7.1 (Conjugates, direct sums and blocks). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M and (K(γ)),N(K(\gamma)),\mathfrak N(K(γ)),N be measurable fields with fundamental sequences (ξn)(\xi_n)(ξn​) and (ηn)(\eta_n)(ηn​).

  1. (Conjugate field) Let H(γ)‾\overline{H(\gamma)}H(γ)​ be the conjugate Hilbert space, the same set with scalar multiplication λ⋅v‾=λˉv‾\lambda\cdot\overline v=\overline{\bar\lambda v}λ⋅v=λˉv and ⟨v‾,w‾⟩=⟨w,v⟩\langle\overline v,\overline w\rangle=\langle w,v\rangle⟨v,w⟩=⟨w,v⟩. Let M‾={ξ‾:ξ∈M}\overline{\mathfrak M}=\{\overline\xi:\xi\in\mathfrak M\}M={ξ​:ξ∈M}, where ξ‾(γ)=ξ(γ)‾\overline\xi(\gamma)=\overline{\xi(\gamma)}ξ​(γ)=ξ(γ)​. Then (H(γ)‾),M‾(\overline{H(\gamma)}),\overline{\mathfrak M}(H(γ)​),M is a measurable field with fundamental sequence (ξn‾)(\overline{\xi_n})(ξn​​). The canonical antiunitaries κ(γ):v↦v‾\kappa(\gamma):v\mapsto\overline vκ(γ):v↦v carry measurable sections exactly onto measurable sections.
  2. (Direct sums) (H(γ)⊕K(γ))(H(\gamma)\oplus K(\gamma))(H(γ)⊕K(γ)) with M⊕N={(ξ,η):ξ∈M,η∈N}\mathfrak M\oplus\mathfrak N=\{(\xi,\eta):\xi\in\mathfrak M,\eta\in\mathfrak N\}M⊕N={(ξ,η):ξ∈M,η∈N} is a measurable field. A fundamental sequence is obtained by interleaving (ξn,0)(\xi_n,0)(ξn​,0) and (0,ηn)(0,\eta_n)(0,ηn​).
  3. (Blocks) A field of bounded operators on (H(γ)⊕K(γ))(H(\gamma)\oplus K(\gamma))(H(γ)⊕K(γ)), or between two such direct sums, is measurable if and only if its four matrix blocks are measurable.

Proof. (1) M‾\overline{\mathfrak M}M is a complex linear subspace, since λ⋅ξ‾=λˉξ‾\lambda\cdot\overline\xi=\overline{\bar\lambda\xi}λ⋅ξ​=λˉξ​, and ∥ξ‾∥=∥ξ∥\|\overline\xi\|=\|\xi\|∥ξ​∥=∥ξ∥ gives (F1). Every section of the conjugate family has the form ζ‾\overline\zetaζ​ for a unique section ζ\zetaζ of (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)). If ⟨ζ‾,ξ‾⟩=⟨ξ,ζ⟩\langle\overline\zeta,\overline\xi\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle⟨ζ​,ξ​⟩=⟨ξ,ζ⟩ is measurable for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M, then so is its complex conjugate ⟨ζ,ξ⟩\langle\zeta,\xi\rangle⟨ζ,ξ⟩, so ζ∈M\zeta\in\mathfrak Mζ∈M and ζ‾∈M‾\overline\zeta\in\overline{\mathfrak M}ζ​∈M. This is (F2). Totality of (ξn(γ)‾)(\overline{\xi_n(\gamma)})(ξn​(γ)​) is the same statement as totality of (ξn(γ))(\xi_n(\gamma))(ξn​(γ)). The last clause restates the definition of M‾\overline{\mathfrak M}M.

(2) (F1) holds since ∥(ξ,η)∥2=∥ξ∥2+∥η∥2\|(\xi,\eta)\|^2=\|\xi\|^2+\|\eta\|^2∥(ξ,η)∥2=∥ξ∥2+∥η∥2. For (F2), suppose ⟨(ζ1,ζ2),(ξ,η)⟩\langle(\zeta_1,\zeta_2),(\xi,\eta)\rangle⟨(ζ1​,ζ2​),(ξ,η)⟩ is measurable for all measurable pairs. Taking η=0\eta=0η=0 shows that ⟨ζ1,ξ⟩\langle\zeta_1,\xi\rangle⟨ζ1​,ξ⟩ is measurable for every ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M, so ζ1∈M\zeta_1\in\mathfrak Mζ1​∈M; similarly ζ2∈N\zeta_2\in\mathfrak Nζ2​∈N. Totality of the interleaved sequence is clear.

(3) The inclusions ξ↦(ξ,0)\xi\mapsto(\xi,0)ξ↦(ξ,0) and η↦(0,η)\eta\mapsto(0,\eta)η↦(0,η) and the coordinate projections are measurable operator fields by (2). Each block is a composite of the given field with these, hence measurable by Theorem 6.2(4). Conversely, suppose the four blocks x11,x12,x21,x22x_{11},x_{12},x_{21},x_{22}x11​,x12​,x21​,x22​ are measurable. Then the field maps a measurable section (ξ,η)(\xi,\eta)(ξ,η) to (x11ξ+x12η, x21ξ+x22η)(x_{11}\xi+x_{12}\eta,\ x_{21}\xi+x_{22}\eta)(x11​ξ+x12​η, x21​ξ+x22​η), which is measurable by (2). □\square□

8. The direct integral Hilbert space

Definition 8.1 (Direct integral). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M be a measurable field, and let L2\mathcal L^2L2 be the set of ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M with ∫Γ∥ξ(γ)∥2 dμ(γ)<∞\int_\Gamma\|\xi(\gamma)\|^2\,d\mu(\gamma)<\infty∫Γ​∥ξ(γ)∥2dμ(γ)<∞. The direct integral ∫Γ⊕H(γ) dμ(γ) \int_\Gamma^\oplus H(\gamma)\,d\mu(\gamma) ∫Γ⊕​H(γ)dμ(γ) is L2\mathcal L^2L2 modulo equality μ\muμ-almost everywhere, with ⟨ξ,η⟩=∫Γ⟨ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩ dμ(γ).(8.1) \langle\xi,\eta\rangle=\int_\Gamma\langle\xi(\gamma),\eta(\gamma)\rangle\,d\mu(\gamma). \tag{8.1} ⟨ξ,η⟩=∫Γ​⟨ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩dμ(γ).(8.1)

We use the same letter for a section in L2\mathcal L^2L2 and for its class, and we also write ∥ξ∥\|\xi\|∥ξ∥ for the norm of ξ\xiξ in the direct integral. When ∥ξ∥\|\xi\|∥ξ∥ appears as a function of γ\gammaγ, or inside a set such as {∥ξ∥≤m}\{\|\xi\|\leq m\}{∥ξ∥≤m}, it is the pointwise norm function of Section 1.

Theorem 8.2 (Completeness).

  1. (8.1) is a well-defined inner product.
  2. The direct integral is complete, hence a Hilbert space.
  3. (Almost-everywhere subsequences) If ξk→ξ\xi_k\to\xiξk​→ξ in the direct integral, some subsequence satisfies ξkj(γ)→ξ(γ)\xi_{k_j}(\gamma)\to\xi(\gamma)ξkj​​(γ)→ξ(γ) in H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ.

Proof. (1) The integrand is measurable by Lemma 2.2(1). It is integrable, since ∣⟨ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩∣≤∥ξ(γ)∥∥η(γ)∥|\langle\xi(\gamma),\eta(\gamma)\rangle|\leq\|\xi(\gamma)\|\|\eta(\gamma)\|∣⟨ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩∣≤∥ξ(γ)∥∥η(γ)∥ and the right side is integrable by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in L2(Γ,μ)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)L2(Γ,μ). L2\mathcal L^2L2 is a linear subspace because ∥ξ+η∥2≤2∥ξ∥2+2∥η∥2\|\xi+\eta\|^2\leq2\|\xi\|^2+2\|\eta\|^2∥ξ+η∥2≤2∥ξ∥2+2∥η∥2 pointwise. Changing ξ\xiξ on a null set does not change (8.1), and ⟨ξ,ξ⟩=0\langle\xi,\xi\rangle=0⟨ξ,ξ⟩=0 forces ξ=0\xi=0ξ=0 almost everywhere.

(2) Let (ξk)(\xi_k)(ξk​) be a Cauchy sequence, with representatives in L2\mathcal L^2L2. Choose k1<k2<⋯k_1<k_2<\cdotsk1​<k2​<⋯ with ∥ξkj+1−ξkj∥≤2−j\|\xi_{k_{j+1}}-\xi_{k_j}\|\leq2^{-j}∥ξkj+1​​−ξkj​​∥≤2−j, and put G(γ)=∑j≥1∥ξkj+1(γ)−ξkj(γ)∥∈[0,∞]. G(\gamma)=\sum_{j\geq1}\|\xi_{k_{j+1}}(\gamma)-\xi_{k_j}(\gamma)\|\in[0,\infty]. G(γ)=j≥1∑​∥ξkj+1​​(γ)−ξkj​​(γ)∥∈[0,∞]. GGG is measurable, as a countable sum of nonnegative measurable functions. The jjj-th term of GGG has norm ∥ξkj+1−ξkj∥≤2−j\|\xi_{k_{j+1}}-\xi_{k_j}\|\leq2^{-j}∥ξkj+1​​−ξkj​​∥≤2−j in L2(Γ,μ)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)L2(Γ,μ). By Minkowski's inequality in L2(Γ,μ)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)L2(Γ,μ) and monotone convergence, ∥G∥L2≤∑j2−j≤1\|G\|_{L^2}\leq\sum_j2^{-j}\leq1∥G∥L2​≤∑j​2−j≤1. So N={G=∞}N=\{G=\infty\}N={G=∞} is a measurable null set. For γ∉N\gamma\notin Nγ∈/N, the sequence (ξkj(γ))j(\xi_{k_j}(\gamma))_j(ξkj​​(γ))j​ is Cauchy in H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ), because the distances between consecutive terms have a finite sum. Let ξ(γ)\xi(\gamma)ξ(γ) be its limit, and set ξ(γ)=0\xi(\gamma)=0ξ(γ)=0 on NNN. Then ξ\xiξ is the pointwise limit of the sections 1Γ∖N ξkj1_{\Gamma\setminus N}\,\xi_{k_j}1Γ∖N​ξkj​​, so ξ∈M\xi\in\mathfrak Mξ∈M by Lemma 2.2(2)–(3). For each iii, Fatou's lemma gives ∫∥ξ−ξki∥2 dμ≤lim inf⁡j→∞∫∥ξkj−ξki∥2 dμ=lim inf⁡j→∞∥ξkj−ξki∥2. \int\|\xi-\xi_{k_i}\|^2\,d\mu\leq\liminf_{j\to\infty}\int\|\xi_{k_j}-\xi_{k_i}\|^2\,d\mu=\liminf_{j\to\infty}\|\xi_{k_j}-\xi_{k_i}\|^2 . ∫∥ξ−ξki​​∥2dμ≤j→∞liminf​∫∥ξkj​​−ξki​​∥2dμ=j→∞liminf​∥ξkj​​−ξki​​∥2. The right side is finite, and it tends to 000 as i→∞i\to\inftyi→∞ because the sequence is Cauchy. Hence ξ∈L2\xi\in\mathcal L^2ξ∈L2 and ξki→ξ\xi_{k_i}\to\xiξki​​→ξ. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges, so ξk→ξ\xi_k\to\xiξk​→ξ.

(3) A convergent sequence is Cauchy. Applied to (ξk)(\xi_k)(ξk​), the proof of (2) produces a subsequence that converges at almost every point to a section representing the limit of the sequence, and that limit is ξ\xiξ. □\square□

9. Diagonal operators, localization and separability

Theorem 9.1 (Diagonal operators, localization, separability). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M be a measurable field.

  1. (Diagonal operators) For f∈L∞(Γ,μ)f\in L^\infty(\Gamma,\mu)f∈L∞(Γ,μ), the formula (mfξ)(γ)=f(γ)ξ(γ)(m_f\xi)(\gamma)=f(\gamma)\xi(\gamma)(mf​ξ)(γ)=f(γ)ξ(γ) defines a bounded operator on the direct integral with ∥mf∥≤∥f∥∞\|m_f\|\leq\|f\|_\infty∥mf​∥≤∥f∥∞​. The map f↦mff\mapsto m_ff↦mf​ is a unital ∗*∗-homomorphism.
  2. (Finite-measure localization) Let (ξn)(\xi_n)(ξn​) be a fundamental sequence. For every E∈ΣE\in\SigmaE∈Σ with μ(E)<∞\mu(E)<\inftyμ(E)<∞ and every n,mn,mn,m, the section 1E∩{∥ξn∥≤m} ξn1_{E\cap\{\|\xi_n\|\leq m\}}\,\xi_n1E∩{∥ξn​∥≤m}​ξn​ belongs to L2\mathcal L^2L2. (Separability) Suppose Σ\SigmaΣ is countably generated modulo μ\muμ-null sets: there is a countable algebra A⊆Σ\mathcal A\subseteq\SigmaA⊆Σ such that every set in Σ\SigmaΣ differs by a null set from a set in the σ\sigmaσ-algebra generated by A\mathcal AA. This holds, for example, on a standard Borel space. Then the direct integral is separable.

Proof. (1) fξ∈Mf\xi\in\mathfrak Mfξ∈M by Lemma 2.2(2), and ∥fξ∥2≤∥f∥∞2∥ξ∥2\|f\xi\|^2\leq\|f\|_\infty^2\|\xi\|^2∥fξ∥2≤∥f∥∞2​∥ξ∥2 pointwise almost everywhere. Pointwise, ⟨fξ,η⟩=⟨ξ,fˉη⟩\langle f\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle\xi,\bar f\eta\rangle⟨fξ,η⟩=⟨ξ,fˉ​η⟩ and (fg)ξ=f(gξ)(fg)\xi=f(g\xi)(fg)ξ=f(gξ), so mf∗=mfˉm_f^*=m_{\bar f}mf∗​=mfˉ​​, mfg=mfmgm_{fg}=m_fm_gmfg​=mf​mg​ and m1=1m_1=1m1​=1.

(2) The integral of ∥1E∩{∥ξn∥≤m}ξn∥2\|1_{E\cap\{\|\xi_n\|\leq m\}}\xi_n\|^2∥1E∩{∥ξn​∥≤m}​ξn​∥2 is at most m2μ(E)m^2\mu(E)m2μ(E), so these sections lie in L2\mathcal L^2L2. Let η\etaη be a vector of the direct integral orthogonal to all of them. Put hn,m=1{∥ξn∥≤m}⟨η,ξn⟩h_{n,m}=1_{\{\|\xi_n\|\leq m\}}\langle\eta,\xi_n\ranglehn,m​=1{∥ξn​∥≤m}​⟨η,ξn​⟩. This function is measurable, and ∣hn,m∣≤m∥η∥|h_{n,m}|\leq m\|\eta\|∣hn,m​∣≤m∥η∥ pointwise. Since the function ∥η∥\|\eta\|∥η∥ lies in L2(Γ,μ)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)L2(Γ,μ), hn,mh_{n,m}hn,m​ is integrable over every set of finite measure. The orthogonality hypothesis says exactly that ∫Ehn,m dμ=0\int_Eh_{n,m}\,d\mu=0∫E​hn,m​dμ=0 whenever μ(E)<∞\mu(E)<\inftyμ(E)<∞. By σ\sigmaσ-finiteness there are sets FkF_kFk​ of finite measure with union Γ\GammaΓ. Apply the hypothesis to E=Fk∩{Re⁡hn,m>0}E=F_k\cap\{\operatorname{Re}h_{n,m}>0\}E=Fk​∩{Rehn,m​>0}. Taking real parts, the integral of Re⁡hn,m\operatorname{Re}h_{n,m}Rehn,m​ over this set vanishes, while Re⁡hn,m>0\operatorname{Re}h_{n,m}>0Rehn,m​>0 on it, so the set is null. Hence {Re⁡hn,m>0}\{\operatorname{Re}h_{n,m}>0\}{Rehn,m​>0} is null. The same argument applies to {Re⁡hn,m<0}\{\operatorname{Re}h_{n,m}<0\}{Rehn,m​<0}, {Im⁡hn,m>0}\{\operatorname{Im}h_{n,m}>0\}{Imhn,m​>0} and {Im⁡hn,m<0}\{\operatorname{Im}h_{n,m}<0\}{Imhn,m​<0}, so hn,m=0h_{n,m}=0hn,m​=0 almost everywhere. Discarding countably many null sets, we get ⟨η(γ),ξn(γ)⟩=0\langle\eta(\gamma),\xi_n(\gamma)\rangle=0⟨η(γ),ξn​(γ)⟩=0 for all nnn at almost every γ\gammaγ, since every point lies in {∥ξn∥≤m}\{\|\xi_n\|\leq m\}{∥ξn​∥≤m} for large mmm. Totality of (ξn(γ))(\xi_n(\gamma))(ξn​(γ)) gives η(γ)=0\eta(\gamma)=0η(γ)=0 almost everywhere.

(3) Fix an increasing sequence (Fk)(F_k)(Fk​) of sets of finite measure with union Γ\GammaΓ. For EEE of finite measure, ∥1E∖Fk1{∥ξn∥≤m}ξn∥2≤m2μ(E∖Fk)→0\|1_{E\setminus F_k}1_{\{\|\xi_n\|\leq m\}}\xi_n\|^2\leq m^2\mu(E\setminus F_k)\to0∥1E∖Fk​​1{∥ξn​∥≤m}​ξn​∥2≤m2μ(E∖Fk​)→0 as k→∞k\to\inftyk→∞. So it suffices to approximate the vectors of (2) with E⊆FkE\subseteq F_kE⊆Fk​ for some kkk.

Fix kkk. We show first that every measurable E⊆FkE\subseteq F_kE⊆Fk​ can be approximated by sets from A\mathcal AA: for every δ>0\delta>0δ>0 there is A∈AA\in\mathcal AA∈A with μ((A∩Fk) △ E)<δ\mu\big((A\cap F_k)\,\triangle\,E\big)<\deltaμ((A∩Fk​)△E)<δ. Indeed, since μ(Fk)<∞\mu(F_k)<\inftyμ(Fk​)<∞, there is NNN with μ((B∖⋃i≤NBi)∩Fk)<δ/2\mu\big((B\setminus\bigcup_{i\leq N}B_i)\cap F_k\big)<\delta/2μ((B∖⋃i≤N​Bi​)∩Fk​)<δ/2. 10. Decomposable operators

Theorem 10.1 (Decomposable operators). Let (H(γ)),M(H(\gamma)),\mathfrak M(H(γ)),M and (K(γ)),N(K(\gamma)),\mathfrak N(K(γ)),N be measurable fields, and let xxx be a measurable field of bounded operators from (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)) to (K(γ))(K(\gamma))(K(γ)) with γ↦∥x(γ)∥\gamma\mapsto\|x(\gamma)\|γ↦∥x(γ)∥ essentially bounded. (That function is measurable by Theorem 6.2(3).) Then:

  1. (xξ)(γ)=x(γ)ξ(γ)(x\xi)(\gamma)=x(\gamma)\xi(\gamma)(xξ)(γ)=x(γ)ξ(γ) defines a bounded operator ∫Γ⊕x(γ) dμ(γ): ∫Γ⊕H(γ) dμ⟶∫Γ⊕K(γ) dμ, \int_\Gamma^\oplus x(\gamma)\,d\mu(\gamma):\ \int_\Gamma^\oplus H(\gamma)\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int_\Gamma^\oplus K(\gamma)\,d\mu, ∫Γ⊕​x(γ)dμ(γ): ∫Γ⊕​H(γ)dμ⟶∫Γ⊕​K(γ)dμ, and its norm is exactly ess sup⁡γ∥x(γ)∥\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_\gamma\|x(\gamma)\|esssupγ​∥x(γ)∥.
  2. The assignment x↦∫⊕xx\mapsto\int^\oplus xx↦∫⊕x is linear and multiplicative on composable fields, and (∫⊕x)∗=∫⊕x∗\big(\int^\oplus x\big)^*=\int^\oplus x^*(∫⊕x)∗=∫⊕x∗. Two fields define the same operator if and only if they agree almost everywhere.
  3. When K=HK=HK=H, every such operator commutes with every diagonal operator mfm_fmf​ of Theorem 9.1(1). Operators of this form are called decomposable, and the mfm_fmf​ are the diagonal operators.

Proof. (1) xξ∈Nx\xi\in\mathfrak Nxξ∈N by definition, and ∥x(γ)ξ(γ)∥≤c∥ξ(γ)∥\|x(\gamma)\xi(\gamma)\|\leq c\|\xi(\gamma)\|∥x(γ)ξ(γ)∥≤c∥ξ(γ)∥ almost everywhere, where c=ess sup⁡∥x(γ)∥c=\operatorname{ess\,sup}\|x(\gamma)\|c=esssup∥x(γ)∥. So the operator is well defined on classes, with norm at most ccc.

For the reverse inequality we may assume c>0c>0c>0; let 0<ε<c0<\varepsilon<c0<ε<c. The set {∥x(γ)∥>c−ε}\{\|x(\gamma)\|>c-\varepsilon\}{∥x(γ)∥>c−ε} has positive measure, and by σ\sigmaσ-finiteness it contains a measurable set FFF with 0<μ(F)<∞0<\mu(F)<\infty0<μ(F)<∞. Let (ek)(e_k)(ek​), QQQ and vqv_qvq​ be as in the proof of Theorem 6.2(3), and enumerate QQQ. For γ∈F\gamma\in Fγ∈F, let q(γ)q(\gamma)q(γ) be the first qqq with ∥x(γ)vq(γ)∥>c−ε\|x(\gamma)v_q(\gamma)\|>c-\varepsilon∥x(γ)vq​(γ)∥>c−ε; it exists by (6.1). The sets Fq={γ∈F:q(γ)=q}F_q=\{\gamma\in F: q(\gamma)=q\}Fq​={γ∈F:q(γ)=q} are measurable, being defined by countably many measurable conditions. The section ζ=∑q1Fqvq\zeta=\sum_q1_{F_q}v_qζ=∑q​1Fq​​vq​ lies in M\mathfrak MM by the gluing property, Lemma 2.2(4), applied to the partition of Γ\GammaΓ into the sets FqF_qFq​ and Γ∖F\Gamma\setminus FΓ∖F. It satisfies 0<∥ζ(γ)∥≤10<\|\zeta(\gamma)\|\leq10<∥ζ(γ)∥≤1 on FFF, since x(γ)ζ(γ)≠0x(\gamma)\zeta(\gamma)\neq0x(γ)ζ(γ)=0 there, and ζ=0\zeta=0ζ=0 off FFF. Hence ∥xζ∥2=∫F∥x(γ)vq(γ)(γ)∥2dμ≥(c−ε)2μ(F)≥(c−ε)2∥ζ∥2, \|x\zeta\|^2=\int_F\|x(\gamma)v_{q(\gamma)}(\gamma)\|^2d\mu\geq(c-\varepsilon)^2\mu(F)\geq(c-\varepsilon)^2\|\zeta\|^2, ∥xζ∥2=∫F​∥x(γ)vq(γ)​(γ)∥2dμ≥(c−ε)2μ(F)≥(c−ε)2∥ζ∥2, with ∥ζ∥>0\|\zeta\|>0∥ζ∥>0. So the norm is at least c−εc-\varepsilonc−ε.

(2) Linearity and multiplicativity hold pointwise. For the adjoint, x∗x^*x∗ is measurable by Theorem 6.2(2) and has the same norm function, and ⟨xξ,η⟩=∫⟨x(γ)ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩dμ=∫⟨ξ(γ),x(γ)∗η(γ)⟩dμ\langle x\xi,\eta\rangle=\int\langle x(\gamma)\xi(\gamma),\eta(\gamma)\rangle d\mu=\int\langle\xi(\gamma),x(\gamma)^*\eta(\gamma)\rangle d\mu⟨xξ,η⟩=∫⟨x(γ)ξ(γ),η(γ)⟩dμ=∫⟨ξ(γ),x(γ)∗η(γ)⟩dμ. Fields that agree almost everywhere clearly define the same operator. Conversely, if two fields xxx and yyy define the same operator, the norm formula (1) applied to x−yx-yx−y gives x(γ)=y(γ)x(\gamma)=y(\gamma)x(γ)=y(γ) almost everywhere.

(3) Pointwise, x(γ)(f(γ)v)=f(γ)x(γ)vx(\gamma)(f(\gamma)v)=f(\gamma)x(\gamma)vx(γ)(f(γ)v)=f(γ)x(γ)v. □\square□

Remark 10.2 (The converse). The converse of Theorem 10.1(3) also holds: every bounded operator on the direct integral that commutes with all diagonal operators is decomposable. It is proved in Decomposable operators and the diagonal algebra.

11. Examples

Example 11.1 (Countable base). Let Γ\GammaΓ be countable, Σ\SigmaΣ all subsets, and μ\muμ a measure with 0<μ({γ})<∞0<\mu(\{\gamma\})<\infty0<μ({γ})<∞ for every γ\gammaγ. Let H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ) be arbitrary separable Hilbert spaces. With M\mathfrak MM all sections, (F1) and (F2) hold trivially, since every function on Γ\GammaΓ is measurable. For (F3), choose a dense sequence (dγ,n)n(d_{\gamma,n})_n(dγ,n​)n​ in each H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ), with dγ,n=0d_{\gamma,n}=0dγ,n​=0 if H(γ)=0H(\gamma)=0H(γ)=0, and let ξn(γ)=dγ,n\xi_n(\gamma)=d_{\gamma,n}ξn​(γ)=dγ,n​. The direct integral is the Hilbert direct sum ⨁γH(γ)\bigoplus_\gamma H(\gamma)⨁γ​H(γ), with inner product weighted by μ({γ})\mu(\{\gamma\})μ({γ}). The map ξ↦(μ({γ})1/2ξ(γ))γ\xi\mapsto(\mu(\{\gamma\})^{1/2}\xi(\gamma))_\gammaξ↦(μ({γ})1/2ξ(γ))γ​ is a unitary onto the unweighted sum. The diagonal operators are the bounded scalar sequences, acting on each summand by multiplication.

Example 11.2 (Constant field). Let H(γ)=KH(\gamma)=\mathcal KH(γ)=K for a fixed separable K\mathcal KK with orthonormal basis (εk)(\varepsilon_k)(εk​), and let M\mathfrak MM be generated by the constant sections εk\varepsilon_kεk​ as in Theorem 3.1(4). The measurable sections are the maps with measurable coordinates, equivalently, by Pettis's theorem, the Borel (or weakly measurable) maps Γ→K\Gamma\to\mathcal KΓ→K. The direct integral is the space L2(Γ,μ;K)L^2(\Gamma,\mu;\mathcal K)L2(Γ,μ;K) of classes of such maps ξ\xiξ with ∫∥ξ(γ)∥2 dμ<∞\int\|\xi(\gamma)\|^2\,d\mu<\infty∫∥ξ(γ)∥2dμ<∞. The map f⊗v↦(γ↦f(γ)v)f\otimes v\mapsto(\gamma\mapsto f(\gamma)v)f⊗v↦(γ↦f(γ)v) extends to a unitary L2(Γ,μ)⊗K≅L2(Γ,μ;K)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)\otimes\mathcal K\cong L^2(\Gamma,\mu;\mathcal K)L2(Γ,μ)⊗K≅L2(Γ,μ;K). Indeed, it preserves the inner products of elementary tensors, so it extends to an isometry. For any orthonormal basis (gi)(g_i)(gi​) of L2(Γ,μ)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)L2(Γ,μ), it carries the orthonormal basis (gi⊗εk)(g_i\otimes\varepsilon_k)(gi​⊗εk​) onto the orthonormal family (giεk)(g_i\varepsilon_k)(gi​εk​), which is complete: if ξ\xiξ is orthogonal to every giεkg_i\varepsilon_kgi​εk​, then each coordinate ⟨ξ,εk⟩∈L2(Γ,μ)\langle\xi,\varepsilon_k\rangle\in L^2(\Gamma,\mu)⟨ξ,εk​⟩∈L2(Γ,μ) is orthogonal to every gig_igi​, so ξ=0\xi=0ξ=0 almost everywhere. So the isometry is onto.

Example 11.3 (Varying dimension). Let Γ=(0,1]\Gamma=(0,1]Γ=(0,1] with Lebesgue measure, and d(γ)=kd(\gamma)=kd(γ)=k for γ∈(1k+1,1k]\gamma\in(\tfrac1{k+1},\tfrac1k]γ∈(k+11​,k1​]. Let H(γ)=Cd(γ)H(\gamma)=\mathbb C^{d(\gamma)}H(γ)=Cd(γ), and let ξn(γ)\xi_n(\gamma)ξn​(γ) be the nnn-th standard basis vector if n≤d(γ)n\leq d(\gamma)n≤d(γ), else 000. The Gram functions ⟨ξn,ξm⟩=δnm1{d≥n}\langle\xi_n,\xi_m\rangle=\delta_{nm}1_{\{d\geq n\}}⟨ξn​,ξm​⟩=δnm​1{d≥n}​ are measurable, so Theorem 3.1(4) produces a measurable field. The sets of constant dimension in Theorem 5.1 are the intervals Γk=(1k+1,1k]\Gamma_k=(\tfrac1{k+1},\tfrac1k]Γk​=(k+11​,k1​], and the direct integral is ⨁kL2(Γk)⊗Ck\bigoplus_kL^2(\Gamma_k)\otimes\mathbb C^k⨁k​L2(Γk​)⊗Ck. The field x(γ)=diag⁡(1,12,…,1d(γ))x(\gamma)=\operatorname{diag}(1,\tfrac12,\ldots,\tfrac1{d(\gamma)})x(γ)=diag(1,21​,…,d(γ)1​) is measurable by Theorem 6.2(1), since xξn=1nξnx\xi_n=\tfrac1n\xi_nxξn​=n1​ξn​. Its norm function is identically 111, so the decomposable operator ∫⊕x\int^\oplus x∫⊕x has norm 111 by Theorem 10.1(1). The inverse field x(γ)−1x(\gamma)^{-1}x(γ)−1 has norm d(γ)d(\gamma)d(γ), which is unbounded. So a measurable field of invertible operators need not define a bounded decomposable inverse.

Example 11.4 (GNS spaces of a separable C*-algebra). Let AAA be a separable C*-algebra with a dense sequence (xn)(x_n)(xn​), and let Q(A)={φ∈A+∗:∥φ∥≤1}Q(A)=\{\varphi\in A^*_+:\|\varphi\|\leq1\}Q(A)={φ∈A+∗​:∥φ∥≤1} be its quasi-state space. It is a weak*-closed subset of the closed unit ball of A∗A^*A∗, so it is compact and metrizable in the weak* topology (see Background used without proof). Give it a finite positive Borel measure μ\muμ. For φ∈Q(A)\varphi\in Q(A)φ∈Q(A), let H(φ)H(\varphi)H(φ) be the GNS space of φ\varphiφ and ηφ:A→H(φ)\eta_\varphi:A\to H(\varphi)ηφ​:A→H(φ) the canonical map, so that ⟨ηφ(x),ηφ(y)⟩=φ(y∗x)\langle\eta_\varphi(x),\eta_\varphi(y)\rangle=\varphi(y^*x)⟨ηφ​(x),ηφ​(y)⟩=φ(y∗x). The sections ξn(φ)=ηφ(xn)\xi_n(\varphi)=\eta_\varphi(x_n)ξn​(φ)=ηφ​(xn​) have Gram functions φ↦φ(xm∗xn)\varphi\mapsto\varphi(x_m^*x_n)φ↦φ(xm∗​xn​), which are weak*-continuous, hence Borel. They are total in every fibre: ηφ(A)\eta_\varphi(A)ηφ​(A) is dense in H(φ)H(\varphi)H(φ), and ∥ηφ(x)∥2=φ(x∗x)≤∥x∥2\|\eta_\varphi(x)\|^2=\varphi(x^*x)\leq\|x\|^2∥ηφ​(x)∥2=φ(x∗x)≤∥x∥2 since ∥φ∥≤1\|\varphi\|\leq1∥φ∥≤1, so the ηφ(xn)\eta_\varphi(x_n)ηφ​(xn​) are dense in ηφ(A)\eta_\varphi(A)ηφ​(A). By Theorem 3.1(4), there is exactly one measurable field of Hilbert spaces over Q(A)Q(A)Q(A) containing these sections. Its fibre at φ=0\varphi=0φ=0 is the zero space.

12. Exercises

Exercise 12.1 (Saturation cannot be dropped). On Γ=[0,1]\Gamma=[0,1]Γ=[0,1] with Lebesgue measure and H(γ)=CH(\gamma)=\mathbb CH(γ)=C, let M0\mathfrak M_0M0​ be the constant sections. Show that M0\mathfrak M_0M0​ satisfies (F1) and (F3) but not (F2), and identify the unique measurable field containing it.

Solution. Norms of constant sections are constant, and the section 111 is fundamental. The section γ↦γ\gamma\mapsto\gammaγ↦γ has measurable inner product γcˉ\gamma\bar cγcˉ with every constant ccc, yet is not constant, so (F2) fails. By Theorem 3.1(4) with fundamental sequence (1)(1)(1), the unique measurable field containing M0\mathfrak M_0M0​ consists of all measurable functions [0,1]→C[0,1]\to\mathbb C[0,1]→C.

Exercise 12.2 (Norm of a diagonal operator). Show that ∥mf∥=ess sup⁡{∣f(γ)∣: H(γ)≠0}\|m_f\|=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}\{|f(\gamma)|:\ H(\gamma)\neq0\}∥mf​∥=esssup{∣f(γ)∣: H(γ)=0}. In particular, mf=0m_f=0mf​=0 if and only if f=0f=0f=0 almost everywhere on {dim⁡H≥1}\{\dim H\geq1\}{dimH≥1}.

Solution. The scalar field x(γ)=f(γ)1H(γ)x(\gamma)=f(\gamma)1_{H(\gamma)}x(γ)=f(γ)1H(γ)​ is measurable by Theorem 6.2(4), and it defines the operator mfm_fmf​. Its norm function is ∣f(γ)∣|f(\gamma)|∣f(γ)∣ where H(γ)≠0H(\gamma)\neq0H(γ)=0 and 000 where H(γ)=0H(\gamma)=0H(γ)=0. Apply Theorem 10.1(1).

Exercise 12.3 (Graphs of bounded fields). Let yyy be a measurable field of bounded operators from (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)) to (K(γ))(K(\gamma))(K(γ)). Show that the graphs G(γ)={(v,y(γ)v)}⊆H(γ)⊕K(γ)G(\gamma)=\{(v,y(\gamma)v)\}\subseteq H(\gamma)\oplus K(\gamma)G(γ)={(v,y(γ)v)}⊆H(γ)⊕K(γ) form a measurable subspace field, and that the graph projections are a measurable operator field.

Solution. Let (ξn)(\xi_n)(ξn​) be a fundamental sequence of (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)). The sections (ξn,yξn)(\xi_n,y\xi_n)(ξn​,yξn​) are measurable in the direct-sum field of Proposition 7.1(2). At every point they span a dense subspace of G(γ)G(\gamma)G(γ), because v↦(v,y(γ)v)v\mapsto(v,y(\gamma)v)v↦(v,y(γ)v) is continuous and the ξn(γ)\xi_n(\gamma)ξn​(γ) are total. So Proposition 4.1 applies. This bounded case needs no functional calculus. Fields of closed unbounded operators are also studied through their graph projections; there one often knows only that suitable sections are dense in the graphs at almost every point, which is the situation of Remark 4.2.

Exercise 12.4 (Why subsequences). In L2([0,1])=∫[0,1]⊕C dγL^2([0,1])=\int^\oplus_{[0,1]}\mathbb C\,d\gammaL2([0,1])=∫[0,1]⊕​Cdγ, give a sequence converging to 000 in norm that converges at no point.

Solution. Enumerate the dyadic intervals [j2−m,(j+1)2−m][j2^{-m},(j+1)2^{-m}][j2−m,(j+1)2−m], m≥0m\geq0m≥0, 0≤j<2m0\leq j<2^m0≤j<2m, in order, and let ξk\xi_kξk​ be the indicator of the kkk-th one. Then ∥ξk∥2=2−m→0\|\xi_k\|^2=2^{-m}\to0∥ξk​∥2=2−m→0, while every point lies in infinitely many of these intervals and outside infinitely many others, so ξk(γ)\xi_k(\gamma)ξk​(γ) takes both values 000 and 111 infinitely often.

Background used without proof

  • Measure theory. Sums, products, pointwise limits and countable suprema of measurable functions are measurable. The monotone convergence theorem and Fatou's lemma hold for nonnegative measurable functions. In L2(Γ,μ)L^2(\Gamma,\mu)L2(Γ,μ), the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ∫∣fg∣ dμ≤∥f∥2∥g∥2\int|fg|\,d\mu\leq\|f\|_2\|g\|_2∫∣fg∣dμ≤∥f∥2​∥g∥2​ and Minkowski's inequality ∥f+g∥2≤∥f∥2+∥g∥2\|f+g\|_2\leq\|f\|_2+\|g\|_2∥f+g∥2​≤∥f∥2​+∥g∥2​ hold. See Section 2 and Theorems 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 of Measure and Hilbert space tools for Haar integration.
  • Hilbert spaces. Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis, that is, an orthonormal family with dense linear span. If (ek)(e_k)(ek​) is an orthonormal basis of HHH, then every v∈Hv\in Hv∈H satisfies v=∑k⟨v,ek⟩ekv=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle e_kv=∑k​⟨v,ek​⟩ek​, with convergence in norm, and Parseval's identity ⟨v,w⟩=∑k⟨v,ek⟩⟨ek,w⟩\langle v,w\rangle=\sum_k\langle v,e_k\rangle\langle e_k,w\rangle⟨v,w⟩=∑k​⟨v,ek​⟩⟨ek​,w⟩ holds for all v,w∈Hv,w\in Hv,w∈H, with absolute convergence; in particular ∥v∥2=∑k∣⟨v,ek⟩∣2\|v\|^2=\sum_k|\langle v,e_k\rangle|^2∥v∥2=∑k​∣⟨v,ek​⟩∣2. If (fk)(f_k)(fk​) is an orthonormal family with closed linear span KKK, the orthogonal projection onto KKK is v↦∑k⟨v,fk⟩fkv\mapsto\sum_k\langle v,f_k\rangle f_kv↦∑k​⟨v,fk​⟩fk​, and for finitely many f1,…,fkf_1,\ldots,f_kf1​,…,fk​ Pythagoras' theorem gives ∥v−∑i≤k⟨v,fi⟩fi∥2=∥v∥2−∑i≤k∣⟨v,fi⟩∣2\|v-\sum_{i\leq k}\langle v,f_i\rangle f_i\|^2=\|v\|^2-\sum_{i\leq k}|\langle v,f_i\rangle|^2∥v−∑i≤k​⟨v,fi​⟩fi​∥2=∥v∥2−∑i≤k​∣⟨v,fi​⟩∣2. A bounded linear map between Hilbert spaces that carries an orthonormal basis onto an orthonormal basis is unitary. See Theorems 2.2 and 4.1 of Hilbert spaces and compact operators.
  • Pettis's measurability theorem, separable case. Let K\mathcal KK be a separable Hilbert space and f:Γ→Kf:\Gamma\to\mathcal Kf:Γ→K a map. The following are equivalent: (a) γ↦⟨f(γ),v⟩\gamma\mapsto\langle f(\gamma),v\rangleγ↦⟨f(γ),v⟩ is measurable for every v∈Kv\in\mathcal Kv∈K; (b) f−1(U)∈Σf^{-1}(U)\in\Sigmaf−1(U)∈Σ for every open set U⊆KU\subseteq\mathcal KU⊆K; (c) fff is a pointwise limit of measurable maps with finitely many values. [Pettis 1938]
  • Weak* compactness. The closed unit ball of the dual of a Banach space XXX is compact in the weak* topology (Alaoglu's theorem). If XXX is separable, the weak* topology on this ball is metrizable. See Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 3.2 of Weak topologies: Tychonoff, Banach–Alaoglu, Mazur, bipolars, Krein–Milman and Eberlein–Šmulian.
  • The GNS construction. Let φ\varphiφ be a bounded positive linear functional on a C*-algebra AAA. There are a Hilbert space H(φ)H(\varphi)H(φ) and a linear map ηφ:A→H(φ)\eta_\varphi:A\to H(\varphi)ηφ​:A→H(φ) with dense range such that ⟨ηφ(x),ηφ(y)⟩=φ(y∗x)\langle\eta_\varphi(x),\eta_\varphi(y)\rangle=\varphi(y^*x)⟨ηφ​(x),ηφ​(y)⟩=φ(y∗x) for all x,y∈Ax,y\in Ax,y∈A. One takes for H(φ)H(\varphi)H(φ) the completion of AAA modulo the null space {x:φ(x∗x)=0}\{x:\varphi(x^*x)=0\}{x:φ(x∗x)=0}, with the inner product φ(y∗x)\varphi(y^*x)φ(y∗x). See Theorem 5.4 and Definition 5.6 of Building representations from positive functionals.
  • Hilbert tensor products. For Hilbert spaces HHH and KKK, the Hilbert tensor product H⊗KH\otimes KH⊗K is a Hilbert space in which the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and ⟨f⊗v,g⊗w⟩=⟨f,g⟩⟨v,w⟩\langle f\otimes v,g\otimes w\rangle=\langle f,g\rangle\langle v,w\rangle⟨f⊗v,g⊗w⟩=⟨f,g⟩⟨v,w⟩. If (gi)(g_i)(gi​) and (εk)(\varepsilon_k)(εk​) are orthonormal bases of HHH and KKK, then (gi⊗εk)(g_i\otimes\varepsilon_k)(gi​⊗εk​) is an orthonormal basis of H⊗KH\otimes KH⊗K. This is proved in Spatial tensor products of von Neumann algebras.
  • Standard Borel spaces. The Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra of a standard Borel space is generated by a countable family of sets, hence by the countable algebra that this family generates. So it is countably generated modulo null sets in the sense of Theorem 9.1(3), and so is its completion for μ\muμ. See Polish spaces and standard Borel spaces.

Where this leads

  • Decomposable operators and the diagonal algebra proves the converse of Theorem 10.1(3). It follows that the diagonal and the decomposable operators form von Neumann algebras, each the commutant of the other.
  • The Effros Borel structure embeds all fibres into one fixed Hilbert space by a measurable field of isometries, and treats measurable families of von Neumann algebras.
  • Vector-valued functions, tensor products with LpL^pLp, and preduals works with a Radon measure on a locally compact space. When that measure is σ\sigmaσ-finite and Σ\SigmaΣ is the μ\muμ-completion of the Borel sets, it shows that the direct integral of the constant field of Example 11.2 is the space of square-integrable K\mathcal KK-valued functions studied there, with the same vectors and the same inner product.
  • Fields of closed unbounded operators, handled through their graph projections with Proposition 4.1 and Remark 4.2, are the subject of the lesson Measurable graphs and left multipliers in direct-integral fields in the course on modular theory and weights.
  • Beyond these lessons, the theory continues with direct integrals of von Neumann algebras and the decomposition of a von Neumann algebra over its centre; see Direct integrals of von Neumann algebras.
